analysis.one_liner: Imposes patient protections on HMOs, including emergency care without prior approval, mental health parity, and the right to sue for denied care.
analysis.headline: The bill drew only 2 cosponsors, never received a committee vote, and died in three House committees when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set federal rules for how HMOs and other managed care plans treat their enrollees. It would have guaranteed access to emergency rooms and specialists without referrals, required coverage of mental health care on par with physical health care and of prescription contraceptives, barred plans from using financial incentives to encourage doctors to limit care, forced plans to spend at least 85 cents of each premium dollar on medical care, and given patients the right to sue in court, including for punitive damages, when a plan's cost-cutting decisions deny needed care. It also applied to managed care plans serving Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in HMOs and other managed care plans — the majority of insured Americans in the late 1990s. They would have gained enforceable rights: emergency care covered without prior authorization, direct access to obstetricians and standing specialist referrals, coverage of contraceptives and annual mammograms, minimum hospital stays after mastectomies, mental health benefits equal to physical health benefits, an independent appeals process, disclosure of how plans pay doctors, and the ability to sue when a plan denies medically necessary care. Medicare and Medicaid managed care enrollees were covered too, and doctors would have gained protections against being punished for advocating for patients.

how_it_helps.text: Guarantees emergency and urgent care 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, with no prior authorization needed for emergency-room services when symptoms would lead a reasonable person to suspect an emergency.

Lets enrollees see an obstetrician-gynecologist without a referral, obtain standing referrals to specialists, and get referrals to outside providers when the plan has no one qualified for their condition.

Bars plans from covering mental health services less generously than physical health services, requires coverage of prescription contraceptives, and sets minimum 48-hour hospital stays after mastectomies.

Prohibits plans from paying doctors bonuses or imposing penalties to reduce tests and treatment, bans contract gag clauses limiting what doctors can tell patients, and makes such arrangements a federal crime for the plan and its executives.

Requires plans to spend at least 85 percent of premiums on medical care, and gives patients the right to sue for actual and punitive damages when a cost-containment decision denies medically necessary care.
Requires plans to disclose how they pay providers, their appeal rates, and their finances, and gives patients independent peer review of denied claims, with urgent appeals decided within 24 hours.

Protects doctors and other providers from retaliation for advocating for patients or reporting violations, bans 'without cause' termination clauses, and prohibits non-compete restrictions on clinicians leaving a plan.

analysis.who_pays: HMOs and health insurers would bear the cost of the new requirements: more covered services, network adequacy standards, independent appeals, an 85 percent floor on the share of premiums spent on medical care, civil fines from the Health and Human Services Secretary, potential disqualification from Medicare and Medicaid contracts for repeated violations, and court liability including punitive damages. Some of these costs would likely be passed to enrollees through higher premiums, and employer-sponsored plans would face compliance obligations.

drawbacks.text: The coverage mandates and the requirement that plans spend at least 85 percent of premiums on medical care would raise operating costs, which would likely show up as higher premiums for enrollees and employers.

The new right to sue for actual and punitive damages when cost-cutting decisions deny care could increase litigation costs and premiums; this liability expansion was the most contested issue in the broader managed care debate of that era.

Criminal penalties, including up to two years in prison, for executives who offer doctors incentives tied to limiting care go further than typical regulatory enforcement and could chill ordinary compensation arrangements that the bill otherwise permits.
The bill's mandates on networks, appeals, and disclosure would add compliance costs for smaller plans, which could reduce plan choices in some markets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gave patients enforceable rights against the cost-control practices that defined 1990s managed care, at the price of higher premiums and compliance costs concentrated on the HMO industry. The core access and coverage protections were moderate; the punitive-damages right and criminal penalties for executives were the most aggressive parts and would have driven much of the opposition. On balance, for the tens of millions of people in managed care plans at the time, the protections were substantial and the costs were real but targeted.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees, then to two subcommittees in April 1999, and sat there with no markup or floor vote through the end of the Congress in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the bill on March 16, 1999, together with Rep. Martin Frost as an original cosponsor.
The Speaker referred it to the Ways and Means, Commerce, and Education and the Workforce Committees; no single committee controlled it, which typically makes action harder.
In April 1999 it was referred to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment and the Education and Workforce Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations.
That was the last recorded action: no subcommittee or committee vote, no floor vote, and no further action for the remainder of the 106th Congress, which ended January 3, 2001.
The bill had only 2 cosponsors, both Democrats, giving it minimal support in a chamber whose majority party was pursuing a narrower, separate managed care bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Managed care organizations and health insurers, which kept their cost-control practices without the access mandates, the 85 percent medical-spending floor, or court liability. No comprehensive patients' rights law was enacted in that Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters were House Democrats; the bill sat in committees chaired by Republicans, who took no action on it during two years of the Congress.

industries.note: The bill would have forced plans to cover more services, spend at least 85 percent of premiums on care, stop paying doctors to limit treatment, and face fines, Medicare/Medicaid contract termination, and lawsuits with punitive damages. Its gain is the public's cost: plans profit from limiting care, and the bill targets exactly that practice.

industries.industry: Health insurers offering group and individual coverage
industries.note: The bill's requirements attach to health insurance coverage under federal insurance law, so insurers would face the same access, coverage, disclosure, and loss-ratio mandates plus new liability exposure.

Doctors would gain due process before being dropped from networks, bans on 'without cause' terminations and non-compete clauses, equal pay rules, and protection from retaliation for advocating for patients — protections that run alongside patient interests.
